writingIdeas.viewpoint: Cash can be more effective than donated goods after some emergencies.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Where local markets still function, cash assistance gives affected families flexibility and supports nearby businesses.
writingIdeas.argument: A standard parcel assumes that every household requires the same items, although one family may need medicine while another needs transport. Cash allows each to respond to its own most urgent constraint. It can also be spent with local traders, helping commercial activity recover instead of importing goods that compete with it. Cash is unsuitable where supplies are unavailable or prices are being manipulated, so market monitoring remains essential. The best emergency tool should follow local conditions rather than donor convenience.

writingIdeas.topicSentence: Assistance is unlikely to last when recipients inherit a system they did not help design.
writingIdeas.argument: A donor may build a technically impressive water system, but its pumps will fail if replacement parts cannot be purchased locally. Involving local engineers and users at the design stage can reveal such constraints before money is spent. Responsibility for fees, repairs and oversight should also be agreed with an institution that will remain after foreign staff leave. This approach may slow the opening ceremony, yet it increases the chance that services still function five years later. Sustainable aid transfers decision-making capacity as well as physical resources.

speaking.question: Describe a charity or aid project that you think is practical.
speaking.answer: I once read about a project that funds bicycles for community health workers in remote districts. The workers already had medical training, but walking between villages limited the number of families they could visit. A robust bicycle, basic repair tools and local maintenance training allowed them to carry supplies and reach patients more regularly. I find the project practical because it solves a clearly identified transport problem without introducing complicated technology. It also relies on people who already understand the community. Of course, a bicycle cannot replace a clinic or an ambulance, but in the right geography it makes existing health skills far more useful. That modest fit between the tool and the need is what impressed me.

speaking.question: Why do some aid projects fail?
speaking.answer: Sometimes donors begin with a product they want to provide instead of a problem that communities have identified. Projects can also overlook maintenance costs, local skills or political relationships. A school building, for instance, achieves little without teachers and a reliable operating budget. Short funding cycles encourage organisations to report quick outputs such as items distributed rather than harder long-term outcomes. Corruption can be a factor, but it should not become a convenient explanation for every failure. Better consultation, transparent spending and independent evaluation can expose whether the original design was realistic.

reading.title: After the Free Tractors Stopped
paragraphs: Following three seasons of poor harvests, a farming district received sixty imported tractors through an international assistance programme. Photographs of the handover showed polished machines lined beside the provincial office. The aim was reasonable: faster land preparation would allow farmers to plant during a shorter rainy season. Within eighteen months, however, fewer than half the tractors were operating regularly.

An evaluation found no single dramatic failure. The machines were designed for larger fields than the narrow local plots, fuel had to be purchased in a town two hours away, and one specialised filter was unavailable nationally. Training had been given to drivers but not to mechanics. Moreover, the tractors were assigned to village committees without a clear agreement about booking, fees or responsibility for damage. Each obstacle was manageable; together they made use unreliable.

A second programme began with the same agricultural goal but a different question: what prevented timely planting? Farmers identified several answers, including labour peaks, broken animal-drawn ploughs and lack of short-term credit. Instead of distributing one technology, the programme funded local repair shops, tested several smaller machines and created a rental service managed by an existing cooperative. During the first year, only twelve machines were available, yet they completed more field days than the original fleet.

The comparison does not prove that imported equipment is always unsuitable. Some components still came from abroad, and larger farms used the earlier tractors successfully once spare parts arrived. The important difference was institutional rather than national: the later scheme financed maintenance, clarified access and allowed several tools to address several constraints.

Aid is often evaluated by what can be counted at delivery—a sum transferred, a well opened or a machine handed over. These figures demonstrate activity, but continued use reveals whether activity became capacity. In the farming district, the quieter investment in repair skills produced fewer ceremonial photographs and more reliable planting days.
